## Designing approvals for agents that act for people: budgets, previews and when to interrupt

Most agent interfaces still have one permission model: the agent can do everything the person can, because it signs in as them. That worked while agents mostly read and drafted. It stops working the moment they buy, send and sign. In the week of 21 October three launches, from a retailer, a model lab and a password manager, each shipped a different piece of the same answer. Read together, they are the clearest picture yet of what a permission screen for an agent should look like.
What shipped
Walmart Agent Profiles (announced 21 October, launching within a month). Today an agent shopping on Walmart signs in with the customer's account, so its orders are mixed in with theirs. Agent Profiles give each agent its own profile inside the account, with its purchases listed separately. By default every agent purchase needs approval; the customer can instead allow spending up to a limit such as $50, $100 or $200, and Walmart says it may still ask for approval inside that limit. Profiles can be turned off or deleted at any time. Under the new terms, agents never receive card details, cannot add or change payment methods, and may only use the information a task needs. A beta Agent Gateway connects agents over MCP and, in Walmart's example, helps an agent find your usual milk without handing over your whole shopping history.
Claude Duet (research preview, 21 October). Anthropic's proactive agent sends a morning brief, checks connected apps every few hours rather than continuously, and messages you only when something needs your attention; you can tell it what you want to hear about and how often. It reads, drafts and prepares work on its own, but before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document or deletes anything, it shows exactly what it is about to do and waits. Some actions, such as trading securities or moving money between accounts, stay off-limits even with approval, and any connected app can be disconnected. Anthropic says the preview may still misjudge what is urgent and cannot yet show you its browser.
1Password for Agents (October). When an agent hits a sign-in form, 1Password shows a prompt naming which agent is asking and suggesting a login; you approve on your own device, and 1Password fills the form without the credential ever reaching the agent. Its Claude integration goes further: there are no standing approvals, so a new agent session means a new prompt, and released credentials expire with the session.
One early hands-on review of Duet, by Claire Vo and summarised in the FocusHeron AI and Designers newsletter, adds the human side: a proactive agent needs a deliberate rule for when it may interrupt, and slow responses quickly erode the willingness to work with it in real time.
Our take
The three launches agree on more than they differ, and the agreement is a design pattern rather than a security feature. Autonomy is not one switch; it is a setting per action type, with four rungs. Some actions are never allowed. Consequential ones are asked every time by default. Routine ones can run within a budget the person chose. Everything the agent did is visible afterwards in its own ledger, separate from what the person did. The approval itself has to be a preview of the exact action, not a generic "Allow?" dialog: Duet's "shows you exactly what it is about to do" and 1Password's "which agent is asking, for which login" are the two halves of a good approval card.
The quieter lesson is about attention. A permission model that asks for everything trains people to tap Approve without reading, which is worse than no approval at all. Duet's few-hours check-in and per-topic notification settings, and Walmart's budget tier, both exist to reduce how often the person is asked, so that the remaining questions get read. If your product adds agent actions, design the interruption budget at the same time as the spending budget.
Checklist: an approval UI for agent actions
Give each agent its own identity. Show its name and icon on every request and on every action in history, never the person's avatar.
Classify actions before you design screens. Read, draft, act within budget, act with approval, never. Write the list down; it is your permission spec.
Default consequential actions to "ask". Sending, paying, signing, deleting and changing account settings start in the ask tier; the person can loosen it later, per agent.
Make the approval card a preview. Show the exact recipient and text, item and price, or file and change, plus who is asking and why. Offer Approve, Edit and Deny, and make Deny as easy to hit as Approve.
Budgets in the person's units. Money per purchase or per week, messages per day, or recipients outside the team. Show the remaining budget on the card and in settings.
Keep a separate ledger. Agent actions get their own list with filters, an undo or return path where one exists, and a one-tap way to pause or remove the agent.
Set an interruption rule. Batch low-stakes items into a brief, interrupt only for blocked or time-critical work, and let people choose topics and frequency.
No standing secrets. Never paste credentials into the agent's context; hand sign-in to a credential manager and expire access with the session.
Make the approval accessible. A blocking approval is an alertdialog with a clear title, focus on the safest option, and text a screen reader can read in full.
# agent-permissions.yml: a starting spec
agent: "Shopping assistant"
never:    [change_payment_method, move_money, trade]
ask:      [send_message, purchase_over_budget, sign, delete]
budget:   { purchase: "$100 / week", messages: "10 / day" }
auto:     [read, search, draft, add_to_cart]
notify:   { brief: "08:00", interrupt: [blocked, deadline_today] }
ledger:   separate_from_owner
session:  { credentials: via_password_manager, expire: on_end }
How UI Hub helps
The building blocks for this UI already exist. Our post on shadcn Trace and AI Elements covers the Confirmation and Tool patterns that an approval card can be built from, and accessibility in AI-generated UI covers focus and dialog roles. For making the agent itself follow your rules while it builds screens like these, see linting agents onto your design system.

## Your design tools now take orders from agents: Framer MCP, Figma Weave and Runway App Studio

Until recently, an AI agent that wanted to change a website or produce a campaign image had two options: write code from scratch, or ask you to open the design tool yourself. Between 22 and 26 October three creative tools removed that gap in three different ways. Framer let outside agents edit its canvas and CMS, Figma let agents call Weave's image and video models through the Figma MCP, and Runway let anyone describe a creative app and get a working one. Each answers the same question, what may an agent do inside my creative tool?, with a different gate.
What shipped
Framer MCP (22 October). Any client that supports remote MCP servers and OAuth, such as Codex, Claude or Cursor, can connect to https://mcp.framer.com/mcp. After you approve the connection, the agent can create pages and edit layouts across desktop, tablet and phone breakpoints using the project's existing styles and components, manage CMS collections and items, and review metadata, headings and alt text. It acts with your account's permissions. Changes stay in the project, or on a branch, until someone publishes; the agent can publish, but only if you explicitly ask. Framer's branches show a diff under Review Changes, and applying a branch to main is a separate step from publishing main.
Figma Weave through the Figma MCP (26 October). With a paid standalone Weave account linked to Figma, an external agent can run a Weave model such as Seedance, Kling or Nano Banana directly, or run a published Weave tool, which is Weave's word for a published workflow such as a product-mockup generator. Runs spend Weave credits, not Figma AI credits. Before a paid run the tool returns a cost-confirmation status and the agent must show you the credit cost and get a yes; workflows whose cost depends on a dynamic iterator say up front that the cost can't be quoted. Private tools are invisible to agents, and creating or editing workflows over MCP is not supported yet.
Runway App Studio (26 October). You describe a tool in plain language and Runway's builder agent plans, designs and deploys an app with its own interface that generates images, video and audio from your Brand Kits, Workflows and assets. Early in the build it asks you to pick one of three colour schemes and can take your logo. An app is a private preview until you publish it to yourself, your workspace or specific people; you can roll back to earlier versions, the code stays inspectable, and each app shows its own credit usage. Launch examples include Precise Edit, which retouches only the region you mark, and AutoComp, which swaps a product into existing footage.
Our take
These are three rungs of the same ladder. At the bottom, the agent drives the canvas (Framer): it can touch anything you can, so the safety comes from where its work lands, a branch with a reviewable diff, and from publishing being a separate, explicit act. In the middle, the agent calls a published workflow (Weave): it cannot change how the asset is made, only fill in the inputs someone else designed, and every paid run passes a price check. At the top, the workflow becomes an app for people (App Studio): the agent's work is the tool itself, and the guardrails are the Brand Kit it reads, the audience it is published to and the version you can roll back to.
The practical lesson for design teams is that the valuable artefact is moving from the prompt to the published workflow. A prompt that produced a good hero image once is a note; a published Weave tool or App Studio app with fixed references, brand colours and a known cost is something an agent can be trusted to run a hundred times. Framer's version of the same idea is the project's own styles and components, which its agent is told to reuse. If your system is not packaged in one of those forms, outside agents will improvise, and that is where off-brand output comes from.
Two cautions. Framer's agent works with your account's permissions, so an agent connected to a personal account can reach every project that account can. And cost confirmation only protects you if someone reads it: batch runs (Weave allows one to ten per call) multiply quickly.
Checklist: letting an agent into your creative tools
Pick the rung on purpose. Use canvas access for layout and content edits, published workflows for repeatable assets, and an app when non-designers need to run the workflow themselves.
Branch by default. Tell the agent to create a branch before every Framer task, turn on automatic branching to protect main, and review the diff and a branch preview URL before you apply.
Keep publish human. Never include "and publish" in a standing instruction; publish main yourself after review.
Connect the narrowest account. Use a workspace or account that only holds the projects the agent should touch, since it inherits that account's permissions.
Publish workflows, not prompts. Wrap your best image or video recipe as a Weave tool or App Studio app with fixed references, Brand Kit and named inputs, so agents fill in blanks instead of inventing styles.
Set a credit ceiling. Decide a per-run and per-week credit budget, keep numberOfRuns low until the output is proven, and treat "cost can't be quoted" as a reason to run once first.
Review assets like code. Check every generated image or page in light and dark themes, at 375 px, for alt text and contrast, before it enters a library or CMS.
Log what the agent made. Keep a list of agent-generated pages, CMS items and assets with the prompt, workflow version and credit cost, so you can find and replace them later.
# creative-agent-policy.yml: a starting spec
framer:
  connect: https://mcp.framer.com/mcp   # OAuth, workspace account only
  always_branch: true
  publish: human_only
  review: [diff, branch_preview_url, 375px, dark_mode]
weave:
  allow: published_tools_only           # no raw model runs in production
  confirm_cost: always
  max_runs_per_call: 2
  weekly_credit_budget: 500
app_studio:
  audience_default: only_me             # widen after review
  brand_kit: required
log: [page, cms_item, asset, prompt, workflow_version, credits]
How UI Hub helps
An agent can only reuse styles that are written down. Our posts on design tokens for agents and linting agents onto your design system cover how to package them, and layers, brand kits and JSON for AI visuals covers the brand-kit side of generated images. For the approval step itself, see designing approvals for agents; for Figma's other agent features, see Figma code layers and Specs.

## Point, don’t describe: visual prompts for UI edits in Cursor, v0 and Lovable

“Make the second card match the first, but tighter” is a hard sentence for a coding agent. Which second card? Tighter how? The agent has to search the code for something that looks like your description, and when it guesses wrong you write a correction that is longer than the original request. On 27 October Cursor shipped Annotate, a reworked version of its browser Design Mode that lets you answer those questions by pointing at the running app. v0 and Lovable offer their own version of the same idea. Taken together they show that, for interface work, the useful prompt is becoming a pointer plus a small change rather than a paragraph.
What each tool sends to the model
Cursor Design Mode with Annotate (27 October, Cursor 3.24.18 or later). It lives in the browser inside the Agents Window; click Annotate or press Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + D. You click an element (arrow keys move the highlight to its parent or child), Shift-click to add more elements to the same note, drag to box an area and draw with pen, ellipse, rectangle or arrow, double-click text to edit it in place, open a CSS inspector on a single element, or dictate. For every picked element the agent receives the tag, id, classes, attributes, a selector path, the first 200 characters of visible text, size and position, six computed styles (colour, background, font size, font family, display, position) and, in React, Vue and Svelte apps, the component name and component stack. It also gets a screenshot cropped to the element or to your marked-up area. Notes go out one at a time by default; a Batch edits switch collects them as numbered pins and sends them as one message. Cursor recommends a fast UI-capable model for this loop, naming Composer 2.5.
v0 Design mode. You select an element in the live preview and either adjust it in a panel (typography, colour, background, margin and padding, border, opacity and radius, shadow, text) or type an instruction, and v0 attaches a screenshot of the element to it. When the project uses Tailwind, the panel offers Tailwind-compatible values. Edits stay pending, with undo, reset and a before-and-after toggle, until you press Apply; Apply sends everything to the chat and produces a normal new version you can diff or revert. A Design Mode API lets teams embed the same editor in their own product.
Lovable preview toolbar. It replaced the older Visual edits panel with four modes: select elements (Cmd/Ctrl-click for several), edit text inline, draw an annotation that is sent as a marked-up screenshot (rough shapes are cleaned up), and pinned comments for teammates. Comments are free; sending one to Lovable, selecting, and drawing use build credits. Each account gets 100 free inline text edits per rolling 24 hours, with a shared workspace cap of 2,000.
Our take
The three tools split along one line: does the tool apply your visual change itself, or translate it for the agent? v0 sits closest to a design tool: panel edits are concrete values, the result is a reviewable version, and the model mainly turns them into source. Cursor and Lovable treat your mark as context: the agent still decides what code to change, but it starts from the right component instead of a guess. Cursor sends the richest context, structured element data and the component stack as well as pixels, which is why it can work inside large existing codebases rather than only in a generated project.
Pointing has two blind spots. First, a note captures one frozen state at one width. The agent sees the hover you circled at 1440 px, not the empty state, the error state or the 375 px layout, and will happily fix only what it saw. Cursor’s announcement mentions reviewing designs at different screen sizes, but the check is still yours. Second, direct manipulation produces raw values. Drag a padding to 18 px or pick #3b82f6 in an inspector and you have just written a one-off that your design system doesn’t know about. v0’s Tailwind-aware values help, but none of these tools promise to map an edit to your tokens. Tell the agent to do it, and lint for it afterwards.
Our rule of thumb: point for where, write for why. The mark gives location, the sentence gives intent and limits. “Match this card’s spacing to the one on the left, use our space tokens, don’t change the copy” is a better note than either a drawing or a paragraph on its own.
Checklist: visual notes that land first time
Pick the smallest target. Use the parent and child highlight (arrow keys in Cursor) until the box is the component you mean, not its wrapper or one span inside it.
Use multi-select for relationships. Select both elements when the change is “make A match B”, “remove the duplicate” or “align these”. A single selection makes the agent hunt for the other one.
Draw only for areas. Box or circle when the change is about a region (crowding, a gap, where a new element goes), not to point at a single button.
Write intent and limits in one line. Say what should change, the token or component to use, and what must not change.
Translate raw values into tokens. After a CSS-inspector or panel tweak, add “use the nearest existing token” and let your design-system lint fail on hard-coded colours and spacing.
Batch related notes, send unrelated ones alone. A round of spacing fixes on one screen is one batch; a copy fix and a layout change on different pages are separate notes the agent can run in parallel.
Re-check the other states. After each round, look at 375 px, dark mode, empty, loading, error and keyboard focus. The note only showed one of them.
Review the diff, not just the preview. Hot reload shows that it looks right. The diff shows whether the agent changed a shared component that ten other pages use.
# a visual note that works (target + intent + limits)
target:  PricingCard[plan="Pro"]  + PricingCard[plan="Team"]   # multi-select
change:  make Team match Pro: same padding, same badge position
use:     --space-6 for padding, Badge variant="outline"
keep:    copy, prices, button labels
check:   375px stack, dark mode, focus ring on CTA
How UI Hub helps
Pointing only stays on-brand if the agent has tokens to map onto. Our post on design tokens for agents covers how to write them down, and linting agents onto your design system covers catching the one-off values that visual edits produce. For the tools themselves, see v0 in practice and Lovable and Bolt; for the states a single note won’t show, see accessibility in AI-generated UI.

- Design mode — v0 Docs: https://v0.app/docs/design-mode
- Edit from the preview — Lovable Documentation: https://docs.lovable.dev/features/visual-edit

## GitHub Replica: AI prototypes that start from your design system, not a blank page

Most prompt-to-UI tools start from a blank page and a model’s idea of what a “clean SaaS app” looks like. You get something polished and generic, and the first hour of review is spent explaining that your product doesn’t have that sidebar, that button style or that kind of empty state. On 28 October GitHub open-sourced Replica, a prototyping tool built by GitHub Design and Microsoft CoreAI Design, which tries to fix the order of operations: designers write and approve the rules first, then anyone on the team prototypes inside them.
What Replica is
Where it runs. Inside the GitHub Copilot app. A plugin adds a Replica canvas that shows your running prototype next to the conversation, so you describe a change, try it, and refine it in one place. It is MIT-licensed and maintained by GitHub staff.
Four parts. Starters (a Minimal app to adapt to your own system, or a CoreAI Sandbox with Microsoft’s CoreAI design system already wired in), the canvas plugin, an optional self-hosted Replica Hub for publishing and comments, and a GitHub build action that only matters once you publish.
Local first. A local prototype needs the Copilot app, Git, Node.js and npm on macOS or Linux. No Hub, Docker, domain or GitHub repository is required. Hub needs a Linux server, a dedicated domain with wildcard DNS and HTTPS, and GitHub approvals, and your organisation runs it, not GitHub.
Models. GitHub-hosted models with a Copilot plan, or your own model provider (public preview, provider’s terms apply). Viewing or reviewing a finished prototype needs no Copilot subscription.
The interesting part: guidance as a reviewed artifact
You run /setup-skills, point Copilot at approved sources (product docs, design-system docs, component and token packages), and it drafts guidance. The docs are explicit that drafting does not activate anything: designers and design-system maintainers review the drafts, and activation is a separate approval. The result is a set of context files, each owning one concern: DESIGN-SYSTEM.md for components, tokens and patterns, PRODUCT-DESIGN.md for scenarios and state behaviour, RESPONSIVE-DESIGN.md for widths, plus accessibility, browser validation, seed data and repository rules.
The bundled skills are strict about how they use that context. The design-system review skill reads only the active folder, never drafts. A rule labelled proposed-default is treated as a proposal, not policy. And when required evidence is missing, the check is marked manual, never pass; the skill is told not to guess components or tokens. The template for DESIGN-SYSTEM.md also rejects lazy context: “TextInput exists” is not an answer to how validation errors are shown.
There is a feedback loop too. With Hub connected, /review-hub-feedback looks for recurring themes across prototype reviews, and /prepare-feedback-proposals turns chosen findings into proposed guidance edits, each shown before you approve it. Comments improve the rules, not just the one prototype that got them.
Our take
Replica is less a new generator than a workflow wrapped around one: branch per prototype, sample data only, ask before committing, never push or publish without approval. That is the right shape for teams where a PM or engineer prototypes alongside designers. The strongest idea is portable: split guidance by owner, separate draft from active, and make “I don’t know” visible. Most agent context files we see are one long, unreviewed AGENTS.md that nobody owns and every agent treats as gospel.
The costs are real. It assumes the Copilot app (macOS or Linux) and, for sharing, someone willing to operate a Hub with wildcard DNS. The canvas proxies the preview from a different origin, so apps that depend on their own origin for storage or sign-in may need extra work. And the docs themselves warn about the failure we see most often in AI-built UI: the agent using similar-looking replacements instead of your real components. Guidance lowers that risk; it does not remove it, so check imports, not screenshots.
Checklist: design-system-first prototyping (with or without Replica)
Split guidance into owned files. Design system, product behaviour, responsive widths, accessibility, seed data and repository rules each get one file and one owner.
Give every rule a condition and evidence. “Use Banner for page-level errors, InlineMessage inside forms — see docs link” beats “use our components”.
Keep drafts out of active context. Agent-written guidance goes to a drafts folder until a designer approves it; label unreviewed defaults as proposed.
Make unknowns visible. If the agent can’t find evidence for a token or pattern, it should say so and leave the check manual, not invent a value.
One prototype, one branch. Keep the default branch as the reviewed starting point; never let a prototype rewrite it.
Sample data only. No production credentials or customer data in prototypes, ever.
Verify the real components. Grep the prototype’s imports for your package and wrappers; a lookalike &lt;button&gt; is a failed check.
Route feedback into the rules. When the same review comment appears twice, change the guidance file, not just the prototype.
# .agents/context/  (one concern per file, reviewed before use)
DESIGN-SYSTEM.md      # imports, tokens, layout, forms, feedback — each with a docs link
PRODUCT-DESIGN.md     # scenarios, saving, empty / loading / error behaviour
RESPONSIVE-DESIGN.md  # required widths, what collapses at 375px
ACCESSIBILITY.md      # keyboard, contrast, screen-reader expectations
SEED-DATA.md          # sample data rules (no real customers)
REPOSITORY.md         # required wrappers, branch + commit rules
# drafts/ is never read as active; "proposed-default" ≠ policy
How UI Hub helps
Replica only works as well as the guidance you feed it. Our posts on design tokens for agents and design skills for Claude and Cursor cover how to write that context; linting agents onto your design system covers catching lookalike components after the fact. For how Replica sits next to v0, Lovable, Figma Make and Magic Patterns, see prompt-to-UI tools compared, and for Figma’s own library guidelines, Figma Make and the Figma agent.

## Canva Brush: AI design moves from generating to editing

The expensive moment in AI design is rarely the first prompt. It is the second one: “change only the headline”, and the tool rewrites the subtitle, moves the logo and picks a new blue. On 29 October Canva Research launched Brush, a vision-language model built for exactly that second prompt. Canva’s own framing is the useful part: generating a design is hard, but editing one is harder, because the model has to know what to change and what must stay exactly as it is.
What Brush is
An editing model, not an image model. Brush looks at an existing Canva design, works out how it is put together and applies the change you ask for, from one line of copy to every slide in a deck. It arrived a week after Canva Craft, the company’s image-generation model; Canva’s split is that Craft makes the image and Brush refines the design around it.
It edits by writing code. Behind the chat, Brush runs an agentic loop: it writes and runs code that adjusts design elements, then inspects the rendered page to decide the next step. The result is ordinary Canva layers, so text, images, colours and layout stay editable by hand.
How it was trained. Canva started from an open-weights model and post-trained it on real design and editing tasks, using design expertise and anonymised data from people who opted in, then large-scale reinforcement learning. The reward scores visual quality, whether the layout follows design principles and whether the task was actually done, with “good” defined by Canva’s professional designers.
Availability. Canva Pro, for supported edits in Canva AI: open or attach a design and pick Brush in the Canva AI model dropdown. Wider access is promised but not dated. Still missing, by Canva’s own list: Brand Kit support, referencing attachments, and better handling of image-heavy layouts.
What the numbers do and don’t say
Canva reports Brush as up to 69% faster on general editing tasks and 46% cheaper per edit task than its previous design agent, and says in internal testing it matched or beat that setup on most editing tasks, strongest at restyling and adapting designs to new formats. These are vendor numbers against Canva’s own earlier agent, not a public benchmark, and “up to” describes the best case. The more telling detail is why Canva cares: at hundreds of millions of users, a few cents per edit decides whether a feature can ship to everyone. A small specialised model that is cheap enough to run on every edit is a product decision as much as a research one.
Two answers to the same problem
The same evening, Krea launched Ad Studio, powered by its first Krea 3 “expert” model for advertising. You paste a brand’s website, it extracts a brand kit (logo, colours, typography) in a minute or two, then generates dozens of ads. Krea claims “full consistency” with the brand; no independent evaluation exists yet. Put side by side, the two launches show where AI design is heading: Krea gets consistency by extracting rules first, Canva by starting from a design that already exists. Both are moving away from the blank-canvas prompt, the same direction we saw with visual prompts in Cursor, v0 and Lovable and JSON brand kits for AI visuals.
Our take
An edit model that works through code on real layers is the right architecture: edits become operations on named elements, which can be scoped, repeated across pages and undone, instead of a fresh image that only resembles your design. The catch for teams is the missing Brand Kit support. Today Brush can see your design but not your brand rules, so “keep it on-brand” is still your job, and the best way to do it is to put the values in the prompt. Treat “restyle” and “resize for Instagram” as the sweet spot Canva itself names, and be more careful with image-heavy layouts until the promised fix lands.
Checklist: edit prompts that change only what you meant
Name the scope. Which pages and which elements: “slide titles on pages 2–5”, not “the deck”.
Name what must not move. Body copy, images, logo position, page order. An edit model is only as precise as its “keep” list.
Give values, not adjectives. Hex colours, font names and sizes beat “more premium”, especially while the model can’t read your Brand Kit.
One intent per prompt. Batch only uniform changes (every header); split mixed requests into separate turns so you can check each.
For format remixes, say what to drop. A slide becoming a 1080×1350 post needs to lose text, not shrink it.
Duplicate before sweeping edits. Multi-page changes are where unrequested drift hides; keep the original to compare.
Check the pages you didn’t mention. Look for text overflow, contrast below 4.5:1, broken alignment and changes outside your scope.
Finish by hand. The output is normal layers; the last 10% is faster in the editor than in another prompt.
scope:   pages 2–5 · slide titles only
change:  font → Playfair Display 40 · colour #1F2A44
keep:    body copy · images · logo position · page order
check:   titles ≤ 2 lines · contrast ≥ 4.5:1 · nothing else moved
How UI Hub helps
The “keep” list works best when your values already have names. Design tokens for agents covers writing them down, and linting agents onto your design system covers catching one-off values after an AI edit. For pointing at elements instead of describing them, see Point, don’t describe; for how design tools are opening to outside agents, see agents that drive design tools.

- Introducing Canva Craft — Canva Newsroom: https://www.canva.com/newsroom/news/canva-craft/
- Canva launches AI design editing model ‘Brush’ — Capital Brief: https://www.capitalbrief.com/briefing/canva-launches-ai-design-editing-model-brush-48352e11-c62c-4319-973a-490efa945f92/

# Design encyclopedia entries (specs + notes, full; skills: see raw URLs)

# Spacing & layout

> Use one 4/8-based scale, a max content width, and consistent gutters; spacing communicates grouping.

## Rules
- **One scale:** 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96 px. No one-off values like 13 or 22.
- **Proximity = grouping:** space inside a group < space between groups (e.g. 8 inside, 24 between).
- **Content width:** body text 60–75 characters; page container 1120–1320 px; side gutters 20 px mobile, 40 px desktop.
- **Grid:** 12 columns desktop, 4 columns mobile; align cards to the same edges as headings and filters.
- **Density:** tools and dashboards can be dense (row height 36–40 px); marketing pages breathe (section padding 64–120 px).
- **No dead space:** a card should not have a large empty middle; size containers to content or fill with real content.

## Tokens
```css
:root{--s1:4px;--s2:8px;--s3:12px;--s4:16px;--s5:24px;--s6:32px;--s7:48px;--s8:64px;--max:1320px;--gut:20px}
@media(min-width:900px){:root{--gut:40px}}
```

## Sources
- [Refactoring UI](https://www.refactoringui.com)
- [Apple HIG — Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout)
- [Laws of UX — Law of Proximity](https://lawsofux.com/law-of-proximity/)

# Typography

> Two families max, a modular type scale, tight display tracking, comfortable body leading, tabular numbers for data.

## Rules
- **Families:** one sans for UI (e.g. Geist, Inter), optionally one display serif (e.g. Instrument Serif) for headlines. Mono for code/data labels.
- **Scale:** 12 / 13 / 14 / 16 / 20 / 24 / 32 / 48 / 64. UI body 14–16 px, line-height 1.5–1.65.
- **Display:** large headings line-height 1.0–1.15 and letter-spacing −0.01 to −0.02em.
- **Hierarchy with weight and colour, not only size:** secondary text uses a muted ink token, not a smaller font.
- **Numbers:** `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for prices, tables, counters.
- **CJK:** add PingFang SC / Noto Sans CJK fallbacks; avoid letter-spacing on CJK body text.
- **Line length:** 60–75ch for reading text.

## Sources
- [Refactoring UI](https://www.refactoringui.com)
- [Web Interface Guidelines (Vercel)](https://vercel.com/design/guidelines)
- [Material 3 typography](https://m3.material.io/styles/typography/overview)

# Colour

> Neutral base + one accent; semantic tokens; check contrast in both themes; gradients only as accents.

## Rules
- **Palette:** a neutral ramp (bg, surface, mat, line, ink, ink2, ink3) + ONE accent + status colours (success/warn/danger).
- **Semantic tokens**, never raw hex in components: `--bg --surface --ink --ink2 --accent --line`.
- **Contrast:** text ≥ 4.5:1, large text and UI glyphs ≥ 3:1 (WCAG 1.4.3 / 1.4.11) in light AND dark.
- **Gradients:** restrained: a sheen on one headline word or a 1px border, not full rainbow backgrounds.
- **Avoid:** muddy mid-tones, two competing accents, saturated blue on pure black.

## Sources
- [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
- [Material 3 colour](https://m3.material.io/styles/color/system/overview)
- [Tailwind CSS colours](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/colors)

# Motion

> Purposeful, fast (150–300 ms), ease-out on enter, transform/opacity only, honour reduced motion.

## Rules
- **Purpose:** orientation, feedback, continuity. Not decoration on frequent actions.
- **Durations:** micro 120–200 ms, panels 250–350 ms, page transitions ≤ 400 ms.
- **Easing:** ease-out (or spring with no overshoot) for enter; ease-in only for exits.
- **Performance:** animate `transform` and `opacity`; avoid animating layout properties.
- **Reduced motion:** `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` swaps movement for fades or nothing.
- **One hero effect per page** (beam, spotlight, marquee). Stacking effects looks like a template.

## Sources
- [Emil Kowalski — Great Animations](https://emilkowal.ski/ui/great-animations)
- [Material 3 motion](https://m3.material.io/styles/motion/overview)
- [MDN prefers-reduced-motion](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/@media/prefers-reduced-motion)

# Accessibility

> Semantic HTML, visible focus, names for icon buttons, 24px targets, keyboard dialogs, WCAG 2.2 AA.

## Checklist
- Real `<button>`, `<a href>`, `<label>`; headings in order (one h1).
- `:focus-visible` ring on every interactive element; never bare `outline:none`.
- Icon-only buttons have `aria-label`; images have meaningful `alt` (or empty alt if decorative).
- Targets ≥ 24×24 CSS px (WCAG 2.5.8); 44 px recommended on touch.
- Dialogs: focus trap, Esc to close, return focus. Prefer Radix / React Aria / APG patterns.
- Don't convey state by colour alone; announce async results via `aria-live`.
- Test: keyboard only, screen reader smoke test, 200% zoom, reduced motion.

## Sources
- [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
- [ARIA Authoring Practices Guide](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/)
- [Radix Primitives](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/introduction)

# Dark mode

> A second palette, not inversion: off-black base, elevation by lightness, desaturated accent, color-scheme set.

## Rules
- Swap semantic tokens with `[data-theme]` or `prefers-color-scheme`; remember the user's choice.
- Base off-black (#06070b–#121212), text off-white (#f3f5fb); avoid pure #000 / #fff pairs.
- Elevation by lighter surfaces; shadows barely read on dark.
- Desaturate / lighten the accent (e.g. #2563eb light → #67e8f9 dark) and re-check contrast.
- Set `color-scheme: light dark` so form controls and scrollbars follow.
- Previews and screenshots need both themes; never ship a "dark-only" demo without saying so.

## Sources
- [Apple HIG — Dark Mode](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/dark-mode)
- [web.dev — prefers-color-scheme](https://web.dev/articles/prefers-color-scheme)
- [NN/g — Dark vs Light mode](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/dark-mode/)

# Mobile & responsive

> Mobile-first layout, 44px touch targets, bottom navigation for primary tabs, safe areas, no horizontal scroll.

## Rules
- Design at 375 px first; breakpoints ~640 / 900 / 1280.
- Touch targets 44×44 px; spacing between targets ≥ 8 px.
- Primary navigation: bottom bar (3–5 items) on mobile; top tabs on desktop.
- Respect `env(safe-area-inset-*)` and use `viewport-fit=cover` only with padding.
- No horizontal scroll except intentional carousels with visible affordance.
- Inputs: 16 px font to avoid iOS zoom; correct `inputmode` / `enterkeyhint`.
- Test on a real device size in both themes.

## Sources
- [Apple HIG — Layout](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout)
- [Material 3 — Navigation bar](https://m3.material.io/components/navigation-bar/overview)
- [WCAG 2.2 — Target Size](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html)

# House style: restrained fancy

> The UI Hub house style for sites we build: fancy but restrained, Aceternity / Magic UI / Cult UI quality, dense real content.

## The rule
"Fancy but restrained": polished like Aceternity UI, Magic UI and Cult UI, never loud.

## Do
- Information-dense cards: lead card + bento grid / collage, aligned edges, consistent gutters.
- One or two restrained accent colours; a gradient sheen on at most one word or edge.
- Real content in every cover and preview (real screenshots or meaningful diagrams).
- Refined motion: spotlight on hover, subtle entrance, ≤ 300 ms.
- Light + dark both designed; mobile checked at 375 px.
- 10 languages with automatic default by browser region.

## Don't (rejected in reviews)
- Documentation-site look for showcase pages.
- Big empty cards, blank covers, placeholder blocks, empty middles.
- Rainbow gradients and glow everywhere; glassmorphism as the main style.
- Muddy / dull palettes; misaligned columns; wrapped mid-word headings.

## Process
1. Read the UI Hub resources and skills first; pick a direction.
2. Produce ≥ 6 design options when the direction is open.
3. Build, then self-audit with impeccable / baseline-ui; deliver public link + light/dark screenshots.
4. If it is ugly, throw it away and redo rather than patching.

## References
- [Aceternity UI](https://ui.aceternity.com/components)
- [Magic UI](https://magicui.design/docs/components)
- [Cult UI](https://www.cult-ui.com)

# Lessons: previews and screenshots

> What we learned shipping 2,000+ component previews.

- Capture the actual component, not the marketing hero; crop to the component.
- Store light and dark shots; label "dark-only demo" honestly when the source has one theme.
- Never hotlink: save compressed WebP locally with credit to the original site.
- Re-check crops at card size: blurry or cut-off previews are worse than none.
- Thumbnails of whole sites are fine for "site" cards; component cards need component shots.


# Lessons: getting good UI from AI agents

> Practical rules that made agent-built UIs look designed instead of generated.

- Give the agent a short DESIGN brief with a "never" list before any code.
- Ask for several directions, choose one, then lock tokens.
- Load one direction skill, one craft skill, one audit skill; more causes conflicts.
- Require real copy; lorem ipsum hides hierarchy problems.
- Make the agent screenshot light/dark/mobile and look at them before saying "done".
